subtype: Approach: rebuild a schedule after a salary change [Revision]
passage:
I'm Anirban. For a year I paid my education loan EMI of ₹7,200 without thinking about it. Then in April my salary went up from ₹32,000 to ₹38,000, and I noticed something: my spending had quietly grown to swallow the whole raise. New headphones, more cabs, nothing I could point to.
That was the signal. On Sunday I opened the loan spreadsheet Santosh from my old hostel had helped me build, and changed one cell: EMI from ₹7,200 to ₹8,500. The payoff date moved from March 2031 to around August 2029. I checked with the bank that I could raise it without a charge; they said yes and changed it that same week.
Then I set a phone reminder for October: 'Loan sheet, review.' Every six months now. Not a big overhaul, just a look.
The raise still bought me a few cabs. It also bought me a year and a half.

qa.q: What was Anirban's EMI before the change?
qa.a: An EMI of ₹7,200.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel on noticing that spending had swallowed the raise?
qa.a: Anirban was uneasy and a little annoyed, since the extra money was vanishing with nothing to show for it.

qa.q: What else could Anirban look at in the October review?
qa.a: Whether the new EMI still feels comfortable, and whether changes like rent mean the numbers need adjusting.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban had not reopened the spreadsheet?
qa.a: The raise would probably have kept vanishing into small spending, and the loan would have run on until 2031.

grounding: Shows a borrower recalculating the payoff date after a raise, increasing the EMI a little and setting a six-monthly review.

Manager's note, one-to-one, 16 July. Pankaj, operations team.
Damini's appraisal came through last month, a raise of ₹5,000. Today, in our one-to-one, she asked for ten minutes on something unrelated to work, and pulled up a spreadsheet of her education loan.
She had redone it the night before. With her old EMI of ₹9,000, the sheet showed the loan ending in 2032. She had tried three new figures and settled on ₹10,500, 'enough to feel it, not enough to hurt'. The new end date read 2030. She said she'd confirmed with the bank that the change carried no fee.
She asked whether the review reminder she'd set, every January and July, was too often. I said it sounded about right and asked her to tell me in January how it looked.
She seemed lighter walking out than walking in.

qa.a: She settled on ₹10,500.

qa.a: She seems careful and quietly determined, wanting to push the loan down without making daily life stressful.

qa.q: What else could Damini do at the January review?
qa.a: Check whether ₹10,500 still sits comfortably and whether her costs have changed, and adjust up or down as needed.

qa.q: How does the conversation look to Pankaj, who wrote the note?
qa.a: Pankaj sees a small, well-planned change and supports it by agreeing the review timing and asking to hear about it in January.

The power was out across Hosapete again, so Sudha did her loan planning by the shop's lantern, with her younger brother Tejas counting coins beside her.
'Imagine it's two years from now,' she said, half to herself, 'and I've missed payments. Why?'
Tejas looked up. 'Because you spent it all on sarees.'
'Be serious.' She wrote as she spoke. 'One: the hospital contract isn't renewed. It's only for two years. Two: Appa's knee surgery, which the doctor keeps mentioning. Three: the monsoon fails, the shop's sales drop, and I'm helping at home.'
Each reason got a small line underneath. For all three, the answer was the same. She'd keep ₹10,000 aside in the post office account, not touched for anything else. And on the inside cover of her loan file she wrote the branch manager's name and the bank's number for repayment problems.
'Now you're done?' Tejas asked.
'Now I can sleep,' she said.

subtype: Approach: set up auto-debit with a reminder [Action]
passage:
Madhav, you forgot your EMI date again? Sit. When I was new here, fifteen years ago, Preeti from accounts forgot hers twice in three months. The bank charged me each time, and my father got a phone call.
So I did three things, in this order. First, I asked the bank to take the EMI automatically on the 2nd, one day after salary came in on the 1st. Second, I set a balance alert: if the account went below ₹5,000, my phone would tell me. Third, I stopped telling myself I'd remember.
It worked for two years. Then one month the salary came late, on the 3rd, and the auto-debit bounced. The alert had warned me on the 1st; I just ignored it. So automation helps, Madhav, but it doesn't think for you. Now go and set yours up before lunch.

qa.q: On what date did Preeti ask for the EMI to be taken?
qa.a: On the 2nd, one day after salary came in on the 1st.

qa.q: How might young Preeti have felt when the auto-debit bounced?
qa.a: Annoyed and a little embarrassed, since the balance alert had given a warning that was ignored.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Preeti's story, and what did it teach?
qa.a: The late salary that made the auto-debit bounce; it showed that automation helps but the balance alert still has to be heeded.

qa.a: Probably worried and caught off guard, which may be part of why those missed EMIs stayed with Preeti.

Suraj had two days before his company sent him to a hydro project in the hills of Kinnaur, where colleagues said the phone signal came and went for weeks. His first EMI was due on the 5th, and he would be up there.
So on Thursday, at the branch near the office, he did it step by step. He filled in the auto-debit form so the EMI would leave on the 2nd, a day after salary. He asked the clerk to switch on an SMS alert for any balance under ₹8,000. Then he wrote the EMI amount, ₹7,400, on a card for his wallet.
Raghav, travelling with him, shook his head. 'You'll forget the card exists.'
'That's fine. The bank won't forget.'
On the 3rd, in a tea shop with one bar of signal, his phone buzzed: EMI paid. On the 12th, another buzz: balance under ₹8,000. He'd been spending more on site than planned. He cut back on the canteen extras.

qa.a: The EMI amount was ₹7,400.

qa.a: He was anxious that the weak signal would make him miss the EMI date, so he wanted the payment to happen without him.

subtype: Approach: inversion asking how the offer could be a trap [Thinking]
passage:
Mridul was the senior everyone in the Jadavpur hostel looked up to: good marks, a new phone, always paying for chai. So when he sat on Sahil's bed and said, 'Ten percent a month, guaranteed. I'm only telling a few juniors,' Sahil wanted to say yes on the spot.
Instead he said, 'Let me think tonight.'
After Mridul left, Sahil lay on his back and turned the question around. What would need to be true for this to be real? Someone would have to earn far more than ten percent every month, every single month, with no bad ones. Banks give maybe seven percent a year. If anyone could do this, why would they need hostel students' pocket money?
He wrote on the back of a practical file: 'Guaranteed + huge + secret + hurry.' Every word looked like a warning.
In the morning he told Mridul, politely, that he was out.

qa.q: What return did Mridul promise?
qa.a: Ten percent a month, guaranteed.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when Mridul made the offer?
qa.a: Tempted and eager to say yes, because he admired Mridul, but uneasy enough to ask for a night to think.

qa.q: What else could Sahil do after saying no?
qa.a: Mention the offer to the warden or another trusted adult, since other juniors are being approached and could lose money.

qa.q: How might Mridul react when Sahil says no?
qa.a: He may be irritated or push harder, since the pitch depends on juniors trusting him and deciding fast.

grounding: Shows a student asking what would have to be true for a guaranteed monthly return to be real, and spotting the warning signs.

'Ten percent a month,' Imran said at the bus stop. 'A senior from our college runs it. I'm putting in five thousand.'
Ramesh frowned. 'Before you do, let's flip it. How would this be a trap?'
'It's not a trap. People got paid.'

Pages of people saying they'd paid and been blocked.
She walked back to the pantry and put her phone next to his. Chinmay read for a while. 'The photo looked so real.'

Dear Lalremsiami,
You asked why I've been so quiet since Holi. Here it is, because I'd rather you hear it from me.
That Saturday, three people from my office batch posted screenshots of their gains, ₹12,000, ₹20,000, all from a tip group on a chat app. One of them wrote, 'Last day for new members.' I joined at 9:40 p.m. By 10:30 I had sent ₹45,000, most of my savings from eighteen months of work. I didn't check who ran the group. I didn't ask anyone. It felt like everyone else was already on the train and it was leaving.
Two days later the group vanished. The bank says the money went to an account that has already been emptied. I reported it to the cybercrime helpline, but they told me honestly that recovery is unlikely.
I'm writing so you don't do what I did.
Bhavna

I'm Sumit, Raghav's roommate, and I've watched him use his 'two-day rule' three times now.
The first time, a man called him about a gold scheme, 'offer closes tonight'. Raghav said, 'Call me on Thursday.' The man never called back.
The second time, a college friend was raising money for a food-truck plan. Raghav waited two days, asked for the papers, and then put in a small amount. It's doing okay.
Last week a message said he'd been 'selected' for a crypto pool and had four hours to join. He showed me, grinning. 'Four hours. So it's a no.'
I asked him once why two days. He said, 'When they rush me, I stop thinking. After two nights of sleep, the rush is gone and only the facts are left. If it's real, it waits.'
I can't tell whether he always feels that calm. But I've never seen him move money the same day.

qa.q: How long did the crypto pool message give Raghav to join?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What might Raghav feel when someone rushes him, judging from what he says?
qa.a: He admits the rush stops his thinking, so he likely feels pressured and uneasy, and the wait lets him feel calm again.

qa.a: It gave Raghav time to ask for papers; the genuine offer was still there after the wait, so he could put in a small amount with facts in hand.

qa.a: Sumit has watched it three times and seems impressed, though unsure whether Raghav always feels as calm as he looks.

Monday, 7 p.m. A smooth voice on the phone offers Deepak a 'forex account' that pays double in six months. 'Transfer ₹20,000 by midnight to lock the rate.' Deepak's thumb is on his banking app. Then he remembers the rule he made after his cousin lost money: forty-eight hours of waiting before sending a single rupee. 'I'll decide Wednesday,' he says. The voice turns sharp.
Tuesday, lunch. He tells Nazia at work. 'It sounded so sure,' he says, and hears how thin that sounds out loud. Nazia asks, 'Who guarantees double?' He has no answer.
Wednesday, 7 p.m. The number is switched off. When he searches it, three complaints come up, all describing the same smooth voice and the same midnight deadline. Deepak sits back, heart thumping, and deletes the payee he had half-added on Monday.

Imran had put ₹12,000 into the trading app over a month, money from his work at the family's fertiliser shop in Malegaon. The balance on the screen said ₹19,400. On Saturday morning he tried to withdraw it. A pop-up: 'Pay ₹3,500 processing fee to release funds.'
He almost paid. Then he remembered the last message from the 'support team': 'After this one step, withdrawal is instant.' They had said 'one step' before, when they asked for the 'account upgrade'.
He stopped, and sat on the shop step to think it through. They took money in easily and kept inventing fees to let it out. That wasn't a slow app. That was a trap.
He walked to Sachin's cyber café. Together they took screenshots of every chat and payment, saved them in a folder, and filed a complaint on the national cybercrime portal. Then he went to his bank before it closed and asked them to flag the transfers. ₹12,000 gone, maybe. Not ₹15,500.

In Guadalajara, Alejandro had watched his balance on the investment app climb for three weeks: 8,000 pesos in, 11,200 pesos on the screen. When he tapped 'withdraw', a message appeared: 'Verification required. Pay 1,500 pesos to unlock.'
His sister Dalia, reading over his shoulder at the kitchen table, said, 'Isn't that the second fee?'
It was. Last week it had been a 'tax deposit'. Alejandro stared at the screen and felt something go cold. Each time he paid, the money moved further away.
'I'm not paying,' he said. That afternoon he and Dalia did it in order. They screenshotted every chat, every payment confirmation and the app's page. They filed a report on the police's online fraud website. Then they went to his bank to report the transfers and ask for the receiving account to be blocked.
The 8,000 might be gone. The 1,500 wasn't.

qa.a: 1,500 pesos to unlock.

qa.a: He felt a sudden dread as he saw the pattern: each fee pushed the money further away.

qa.q: Which of Alejandro's steps best limits the harm?
qa.a: Refusing the new fee, then saving the evidence and reporting to the police site and the bank the same afternoon.

qa.q: How does Dalia see the situation?
qa.a: Dalia spots the repeated fee first and stays with Alejandro through the reporting, calm and practical.
